judgments.reasoning_cat1: The amended identification is riddled with scope problems: the first (electronic publications) paragraph carries no class designation at all while the other two end 'in Class 16' and 'in Class 36', 'related topics such as oil drilling, technology and infrastructure' is an open-ended illustrative list, and 'oil pricing worldwide' in the electronic entry versus plain 'oil pricing' in the printed entry invites an argument about geographic reach. The negative carve-out ('not including information concerning asset management and investment advice relating to stocks and bonds') is exactly the kind of boundary term two competitors would read differently.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Background recites an application 'in International Classes 9, 16 and 36', yet paragraph 1's first entry omits any class, a recital-vs-operative mismatch; paragraph 2's covenant is keyed to 'the goods and services as set forth in that application as amended pursuant to paragraph 1', so any gap here propagates into the covenant.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The covenant piles a broad catch-all ('or otherwise contest or challenge', 'or do any act or thing in derogation thereof') onto the specific acts of opposing or seeking cancellation, leaving its reach — e.g. whether an infringement suit over related marks is 'in derogation' — genuinely uncertain. It is also expressly limited to 'the mark PETROLEUM ARGUS as shown in that application', which raises the unanswered question of use of ARGUS alone.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends entirely on paragraph 1's amended identification, and sits against a Background recital that frames the deal only as resolving the extension-of-time/opposition dispute, so the agreement as a whole is silent on marketplace use while this clause arguably restrains it; paragraph 6's entire-agreement clause forecloses resort to outside understandings.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Same structure as paragraph 2 — enumerated acts followed by 'otherwise contest or challenge' and 'any act or thing in derogation thereof' — and it protects rights 'in the mark ENERGY ARGUS' generally while the registrations are for ENERGY ARGUS & Design, a discrepancy a court could be asked to resolve. Whether the covenant reaches use, or only registry proceedings, is not stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Background recital mentions only the PETROLEUM ARGUS application (App. No. 75/337,886) and says nothing about the two ENERGY ARGUS registrations, so this operative paragraph exceeds the dispute the recital describes; it also has no counterpart amendment obligation like paragraph 1, unlike the parallel paragraph 2.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sentence is mechanically broken — 'the performance of shall be governed' omits its object — and the second sentence, 'This provision extends to the United States, its territories and possessions', is opaque: it is unclear whether 'this provision' means the choice of law, or is a territorial limitation on the whole agreement. That geographic sentence is precisely the kind of short, unexplained phrase parties fight over.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against paragraph 1, which describes publications 'reporting oil pricing worldwide' and services delivered 'via a global computer network', a US-only territorial reading of this sentence is hard to reconcile with the covenants in paragraphs 2 and 3, which are not expressly limited to any territory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is short and standard, but 'licensees' as beneficiaries is unusual and undefined, and 'successors' is undefined, so whether a renamed affiliate or a US distributor takes the benefit of the paragraph 2 and 3 covenants is left open. Nothing else defines who counts.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else in the instrument addresses assignment, affiliates or third-party beneficiaries, and the parties are identified only by their 2001 names in the preamble, so this clause is the only bridge to a later corporate successor asserting the covenants — a foreseeable point of contest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line merger and no-oral-modification clause with no defined terms and no internal tension; 'this' plainly refers to the document. Little for a court to construe on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits comfortably with the Background recitals, which are framed as history rather than operative terms, and no other provision permits informal amendment or incorporates outside documents; its only friction is that it forecloses extrinsic explanation of paragraph 1's gaps.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'all their own costs in attorneys' fees' contains a plain mechanical error — 'in' where 'and' was surely meant — which on a literal reading limits the clause to costs incurred in attorneys' fees rather than costs and fees generally. The intended sense is recoverable, but the error is on the face of the text.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision addresses fee-shifting, enforcement costs or remedies for breach, so there is nothing in the instrument to contradict it; the only question is whether it survives a later enforcement action, which the agreement does not address.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'will agree to keep' is an agreement to agree rather than a present covenant, and the exception 'as required by Court order and/or state and federal rules of civil procedure' is loose — rules of civil procedure rarely 'require' disclosure, so its boundary is uncertain. Both features give a court something to construe if either side pleads the agreement publicly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else in the instrument bears on disclosure, and paragraphs 2 and 3 contemplate PTO proceedings where the agreement might have to be produced, a tension the exception addresses only obliquely.
